name: Saint Helena
summary_text: The United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 code of practice on single-sex services do not automatically extend to Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha. Local law governs the territory, and those United Kingdom measures can be applied only by Order in Council, so a visitor should expect the territory's own statutes and practices rather than the United Kingdom framework to determine how single-sex services, records and complaints are handled.  Consensual same-sex activity has been lawful in the territory since 2001, and the age of consent is equalised at 16 across Saint Helena, Ascension Island and Tristan da Cunha. The 2009 constitutional order imposed by the United Kingdom bans discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation territory-wide, and those protections have been in force since 2009.  Same-sex marriage was legislated island by island. The Ascension Island Council approved the marriage ordinance on 31 May 2016 by 5 votes to 0; it was signed and gazetted on 20 June 2016 and commenced on 1 January 2017. Tristan da Cunha followed on 4 August 2017 and Saint Helena on 20 December 2017.  Adoption by same-sex couples has been permitted since 2017. The territory is classified as an Overseas Country or Territory of the European Union, and the applicability of the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights is recorded on that basis.

name: Alabama
summary_text: Alabama is a state within the United States and stands under the federal framework that applies in every state. Travel documents are the sharpest exposure for a trans visitor: Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, and prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas. The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth, and new passports are processed only as M or F according to supporting documents, while passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until expiry. In November 2025 the Supreme Court allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. The ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and Lambda Legal maintains guidance on how name and gender changes interact with federal records. Screening at checkpoints carries an outing risk, since TSA procedures can involve secondary screening, devices and pat-downs that are invasive of privacy. Outside pressure has followed: in March 2025 at least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the United States, and in April 2025 several countries issued advisories about trans people travelling over identity-document and data rules. On the ground, Alabama enacted facility bans in 2022 and 2024. A national assessment published in July 2026 reports that a state bill carries a bathroom ban extending to college campuses, and it places Alabama in its worst-law grouping of legislatively-erasing jurisdictions. Violence risk in the state is documented alongside the legal picture. A national analysis by The Needle gives Alabama a killing rate of trans women of 3.8 per 100,000 per year, described as an undercount floor and computed on a 428-victim base covering 2008 to 2025, and the same analysis grades the state in its worst-law group.

sources.title: Alabama Vulnerable Child Compassion and Protection Act (SB 184)
sources.documents: Criminal ban on gender-affirming care for minors - core trans legal risk and enforcement penalty.
sources.detail: No URL visible. Citation detail visible: Passed early 2022, signed April 8 by Gov. Kay Ivey, effective May 8, 2022; Class C felony for provider giving puberty blockers, hormones, surgeries to anyone under 19, punishable by 10 years prison; 11th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals Aug 21, 2023 allowed enforcement pending permanent decision; trial scheduled April 2, 2024. State hired expert James Cantor; Judge Liles C. Burke gave testimony very little weight.

sources.title: Boe v. Marshall aka Eknes-Tucker v. Ivey
sources.documents: Court challenge to gender-affirming care ban by five parents; scope of parental rights, DOJ involvement, current enforceability.
sources.detail: No URL visible. Citation detail visible: Five parents sued with AG Steve Marshall defendant; state sought all medical/mental health records on gender dysphoria; Judge Burke May 13, 2022 temporarily halted puberty blocker/hormone ban but left surgery ban; summarized in The New York Times as sex discrimination / parental rights issue; Aug 2023 three-judge 11th Circuit panel allowed ban; Sept 11, 2023 rehearing request; Dec 26, 2023 Judge Burke allowed case to continue; Jan 2023 expense review >$1M legal counsel + >$500K experts; plaintiffs withdrew May 1, 2025, ban remained in force.

sources.title: Corbitt v. Taylor
sources.documents: Identity-document rules for trans people; surgical procedure + name-change requirement to amend birth certificate / driver's license sex marker.
sources.detail: No URL visible. Citation detail visible: Alabama allows amendment with documentation of sex changed by surgical procedure and name change; Jan 2021 federal judge ruled surgery requirement violated plaintiff's rights in part under Equal Protection Clause; appealed a month later to Eleventh Circuit by defendants; Eleventh Circuit struck down lower ruling, leaving requirement standing.
